title: $2.43M In Reported Sales In Under 11 Months
description: A Canadian e-commerce brand selling high-value products online, with buyers in several markets across Canada. The brand isn't named, at its request.
issue: The brand needed a way to win online buyers that would scale: catch the people already searching for what it sells, create new demand from people who weren't, and grow beyond its home market.

And it had to work on a small budget. $28,736.09 across both platforms in nearly eleven months, about $89 a day, with no big launches or sale weekends to lean on. Every dollar had to find a real buyer, in a market where each one spends about $200 an order.

goals.title: Capture buyers already searching
goals.detail: Be there when people search for exactly what the brand sells.

goals.title: Create new demand
goals.detail: Reach new buyers who look like the brand's existing customers.

goals.title: Grow beyond the home market
goals.detail: Scale past one city into markets across Canada.

approach.idea: Their buyers spend about $200 an order, so the job was never cheap clicks. It was finding the right people, and letting the data, not a hunch, decide where the next dollar went.
steps: One prospecting campaign, all year. Every dollar of 2026 Meta spend ran through a single, always-on prospecting campaign.
Split by market. One ad set per Canadian market on an equal daily budget, so every market got a fair test.
Look-alikes, not cold interests. Each ad set reached people who look like the brand's existing buyers, instead of guessing at interests.
Google Search for the people already looking. Meta created new demand; Google caught the buyers who were already searching.
Our own video, feeding both. Filmed in person and edited by our team. No stock footage, no recycled creative.
The budget follows the data. More reach didn't mean more buyers, so spend moved toward whichever market proved it could sell.

results.intro_html: About 84.8 dollars back for every dollar spent, across both platforms, at $1.84 a purchase on Meta. One honest caveat: each platform counts its own sales, so a buyer who saw both ads can be counted twice. The $2.43M is the two platforms' combined count, not audited revenue.
results.note_html: Figures are frozen to 20 November 2026 and are platform-reported, as each ad account shows them: Meta on its 7-day click attribution setting, Google on its own attribution, which splits credit across ads. They are not audited revenue or profit. What else helped: the brand's existing customers, without whom there would be nothing for look-alike audiences to copy, and a period that runs into the start of the holiday buying season. The brand isn't named, at its request.
